In a capitalist system supported by nation-states, corporations historically found cash beneficial to drive growth and reach consumers. But in our current era, major firms increasingly regard cash as outdated—something that impedes automation and expansion. Physical currency cannot be integrated easily into global digital networks, so it appears to slow the velocity and scale demanded by modern commerce. Thus, even people who appreciate using cash may eventually be driven away from it by subtle, systemic forces.

We must keep in mind that this shift doesn’t rely on an explicit directive from CEOs or political leaders. Instead, we are all caught in a chain of interdependencies that collectively push society toward cashless transactions. Corporations aim to maximize profit, and part of that formula is removing anything that feels inconvenient or slower than digital alternatives. Over time, these changes form feedback loops: if one major bank closes ATMs, the public is nudged into embracing digital payments. Once that is normalized, more businesses find it logical to announce “We’re cashless,” which further reduces consumer access to cash.

Amazon, for instance, has minimal infrastructure for physical money. Local merchants, hoping to stay competitive, often align themselves with automated payments systems, inadvertently joining forces with Big Tech and Big Finance. A small café that goes cashless is effectively telling customers, “To buy a coffee, you must connect with the banking sector’s digital architecture.” That might feel natural in certain cosmopolitan areas. However, it reveals how commercial norms and cultural trends can converge, gradually sidelining physical currency until it seems antiquated.

In political terms, the ‘invisible hand’ can be visualised like a pyramid: citizens and small businesses at the base, large banks and corporations above them, and the government at the summit. Defenders of the cashless movement frequently assert that they are simply responding to consumer preferences—that if people truly wanted to keep using cash, banks would never scale back ATMs. Yet, critics point out that these companies invest enormous sums in persuading people that digital payments are a boon for speed, efficiency, and safety. Meanwhile, smaller, more independent shops struggle to keep up with the technological demands required to offer multiple payment modes, or they give in to corporate partnerships that promise easy solutions.

The confusion grows because cash itself is a public-private hybrid. It is issued by central banks but prized for its anonymity—a feature that appeals to some libertarians anxious about surveillance. By contrast, digital payment platforms belong to private companies, which can share data with corporate partners or government agencies. This concerns various ideological camps. Some activists take issue with moneyed interests encroaching on our autonomy, while others worry about states using digital footprints to monitor citizens.

The decline of cash arises from overlapping dynamics of profit-seeking, social consent, and technology’s momentum. Some fear offline exchange may soon vanish. No single cabal orchestrates it outright; rather, countless small actions converge to make cashless society feel not only practical but inevitable. Yet, as with any systemic shift, there are those who question whether convenience should override the benefits of tangible currency—particularly the ability to transact privately and without dependence on the digital grid.
passages.V2:
The universe is made up of much more than meets the eye. While telescopes reveal countless galaxies…physicists and astronomers believe visible matter is just the tip of the iceberg, and that some unseen dark matter must be out there as well. No one knows what it’s made of, but scientists are confident it doesn’t interact with light—or else we’d see it. Yet decades of searching have failed to yield any direct detections…leaving researchers wondering if they need new strategies or a rethink of gravity.

The case for dark matter dates back to when astronomers studied galaxy rotation rates and found there isn’t enough visible matter to account for the observed spin…which couldn’t be explained by the stars, gas and dust we can see. Since then, further evidence has come from examining clusters of galaxies... The shape of a cluster can be distorted by the gravitational influence of unseen matter, known as “gravitational lensing,” which supports the notion of dark matter... Occasionally, clusters slam into each other; observing the collision dynamics can reveal unseen matter... This is most dramatic in the so-called Bullet Cluster... where computer simulations suggest dark matter drove the impact as much as regular matter... Yet another line of evidence comes from the cosmic microwave background... which shows “hot” and “cold” spots hard to explain without dark matter.

As compelling as these observations are, they’re all indirect. Scientists still want to detect dark matter particles directly…and for decades, the leading theory held that dark matter was made of “weakly interacting massive particles,” or WIMPs. Because they barely interact with ordinary matter, WIMPs are incredibly elusive. Countless experiments have tried to snag them, but no clear signals have emerged—leading some to suspect dark matter might be something else. “I think WIMPs are falling out of favor,” says theoretical physicist Sean Tulin. One high-profile effort, the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment, recently ruled out heavier WIMPs. Yet lighter ones remain possible. Eventually, searches may hit the “neutrino floor,” where signals from neutrinos swamp any potential dark matter signal. “It’s remarkable they pushed the limit down this far,” says physicist Tracy Slatyer, noting that this brings experiments ever closer to that background noise barrier.

Among the non-WIMP candidates, axions may be the new favorite... If they exist, they would solve puzzles involving the strong nuclear force. Like WIMPs, axions are thought to have formed in the early universe, clumping together and guiding galaxy evolution. They may be even lighter than WIMPs... “Axions are naturally produced in the early universe... The fact that they are much lighter...just means their number density would have to be much higher...” says Peter Graham. Various labs are searching for axions, but with no definitive results so far... Meanwhile, some astronomers suspect invisible “halos” of dark matter surrounding galaxies...

Another possibility—seen as a long shot—is that dark matter doesn’t exist, and gravity needs tweaking... But physicists say it’s not so simple, citing data from galaxy clusters, gravitational lensing and the cosmic microwave background that point toward unseen matter.
passages.V3:
Modern humans descended from not one, but at least two ancestral populations that drifted apart and later reconnected, long before modern humans spread across the globe. Using advanced analysis based on full genome sequences, researchers from the University of Cambridge have found evidence that modern humans are the result of a genetic mixing event between two ancient populations that diverged around 1.5 million years ago... For the last two decades, the prevailing view in human evolutionary genetics has been that Homo sapiens first appeared in Africa around 200,000 to 300,000 years ago, and descended from a single lineage. However, these latest results ... suggest a more complex story.

"The question of where we come from is one that has fascinated humans for centuries," said first author Dr. Trevor Cousins from Cambridge's Department of Genetics. "For a long time, it’s been assumed that we evolved from a single continuous ancestral lineage, but the exact details of our origins are uncertain." "Our research shows clear signs that our evolutionary origins are more complex, involving different groups that developed separately for more than a million years, then came back to form the modern human species," said co-author Professor Richard Durbin... The team's method relied on analyzing modern human DNA, rather than extracting genetic material from ancient bones, and enabled them to infer the presence of ancestral populations that may have otherwise left no physical trace... While the researchers were able to identify these two ancestral populations, they also identified some striking changes that happened after the two populations initially broke apart.

"Immediately after the two ancestral populations split, we see a severe bottleneck in one of them—suggesting it shrank to a very small size before slowly growing over a period of one million years," said co-author Professor Aylwyn Scally... "This population would later contribute about 80% of the genetic material of modern humans, and also seems to have been the ancestral population from which Neanderthals and Denisovans diverged." "However, some of the genes from the population which contributed a minority of our genetic material... may have played a crucial role in human evolution," said Cousins.

"What's becoming clear is that the idea of species evolving in clean, distinct lineages is too simplistic," said Cousins. "Interbreeding and genetic exchange have likely played a major role in the emergence of new species repeatedly across the animal kingdom." So who were our mysterious human ancestors? Fossil evidence suggests that species such as Homo erectus and Homo heidelbergensis lived both in Africa and other regions during this period, making them potential candidates... although more research will be needed to identify which genetic ancestors corresponded to which fossil group. Looking ahead, the team hopes to refine their model to account for more gradual genetic exchanges between populations...

"The fact that we can reconstruct events from hundreds of thousands or millions of years ago just by looking at DNA today is astonishing," said Scally. "And it tells us that our history is far richer and more complex than we imagined."
passages.V4:
The Superiority Objection against humorism is based upon the Superiority Theory, one of the three theories of humor. It rejects humorism as unethical, vicious, counterproductive to social cohesion or otherwise inappropriate due to the superior position that one assumed over the object of ridicule. While the ‘object of ridicule’ oftentimes refers to a person who violates a norm, in the present context of Humoristic Absurdism it is not a person which violates a norm, but reality, by failing to meet our demand for resolution. It is in this sense, according to this applied version of the Superiority Objection, that one assumes superiority over reality in its fundamentally disappointing nature.

An early example of the Superiority Objection can be found in the works of Plato, who observed that the derision inherent to humorous laughter inflicts a “pain in the soul”. In similar opposition, Aristotle even proposed a political measure in relation to the derisive nature of humor. A joke, Aristotle says, “is a kind of mockery, and lawgivers forbid some kinds of mockery - perhaps they should have forbidden some kinds of jokes.”

From a Confucian tradition, a similar objection can be made with reference to reverence: humor may destabilize social harmony given its tendency to exalt the humorist and, consequently, to humiliate the object of such humorous derision, thus lacking proper reverence with regard to the societal hierarchy. These instances of the Superiority Objection can hardly be called comprehensive attempts to evaluate humor in light of the associated derision and superiority. Humanity had to wait for two more millennia for more extensive attempts, until Thomas Hobbes formulated a relatively well-developed exposition of the Superiority Objection. According to him, laughter arises from a sense of sudden glory — a feeling of superiority over others or over our own former selves.

The core of the Superiority Objection is this. As humor is inextricably connected to an asymmetrical relation of assigned worth, conceiving the comical object as inferior and the diverted subject as superior, humorism is tied to a variety of vices. In the most charitable interpretation of humorists, we should assign vanity to the humorist; from the most critical standpoint, it is not mere vanity, but malice or even cruelty. Indeed, scholars pleading the latter verdict can point to the way in which jokes tend to undermine people’s worth, both in the eyes of others and in self-perception.

From a Kantian point of view, this may be seen as a violation of a human being’s fundamental worth, or as the instrumentalization of another person as a mere means to elevate one’s sense of self-worth. From an utilitarian stance, it may be argued that the interiorization of the comical other does serious harm - and it is at least dubitable whether humoristic self-exaltation really outweighs the harm inflicted upon the other, especially considering the supposedly inferior position of the comical object that is already assumed as part of the source of risibility.

Hate is destructive not just to its targets but also to those who hold it. It consumes energy, distorts reality, and fosters resentment. Research shows that people who cling to hate experience higher levels of stress, anxiety, and even physical health issues. Hate undermines mental and emotional well-being. On a larger scale, hate causes social division. It tears families apart, fuels political and racial tensions, and makes it nearly impossible for societies to progress together. Hate-driven violence—including hate crimes, terrorism, and genocide—has tragically shaped history, demonstrating that unchecked hatred leads to devastating consequences. However, if hate is learned, it can also be unlearned. The cycle is not inevitable.
